Title: 9.2 Management Directives for Field Employees
Directive: 9.2MANAGEMENT DIRECTIVESfor FIELD EMPLOYEE-OWNERS____________________________________________________All GSL Field Employee-Owners shall follow GSL’s General Site Work Requirements as directed by GSL’s Branch Superintendent.  All GSL Field Employee-Owners shall follow GSL’s Site-Specific Work Requirements as directed by the job’s Project Manager, Superintendent, and Foreman.General Site Work Requirements for GSL Electric Field Employee-Owners -As a GSL Electric Field Employee-Owner, you are to focus on safety and performing your work as productively as possible.  Without compromising safety, any issues that are restricting productivity should be brought to the attention of your project leadership as soon as possible.You are to immediately report any safety concerns to your project leadership as soon as possible and you shall not proceed with work if you feel it unsafe to do so.  You play a key role in identifying, controlling, and reporting hazardous conditions that may occur or already exist in the workplace.  You are required to follow GSL’s, the General Contractor’s, and the Owner’s safety policies and procedures.You are to be signed in and be ready to begin work at the assigned start time at your designated work area for your given project, ready for stretch and flex, ready to receive layout instructions, and have your tools ready.Wearing your tool belt and bags is required during your work shift.  The workday ends at your designated work area at the end of the work shift.  Ten minutes are allowed for clean-up and completion of timecards. Accurately completing your timecard and signing out are mandatory.GSL does not have scheduled breaks other than lunch breaks, unless required by state law or a specific project. Two ten-minute breaks may be taken during the day to use the restroom, etc.  Breaks are to be taken at a time that will minimize impacts to workflow. Break time starts when you stop working and ends when you resume working.  This includes lunches. Lunchtimes will be scheduled based on project specific needs and requirements. For the 10-minute breaks, you are not allowed to leave the job site.  Leaving the project site for lunch is only allowed if the scheduled time permits.If you need to leave your shift early, you need the approval of your immediate supervisor and the Foreman/Superintendent.  If you need to schedule paid or unpaid time off from work, you will need to fill out a request for time off and it must be approved by the Project Foreman/Superintendent with a copy to be submitted to the General Superintendent. These requests must be submitted two weeks in advance unless unforeseen circumstances arise.  If you are going to be late or absent from work, you must call the designated Branch call-in number prior to the start of your shift.  You should also call your Foreman/Superintendent at the job site before the start of your shift.  The only exception is personal or family emergencies.  The General Superintendent must be informed as soon as reasonably possible. The General Superintendent will then notify the site Foreman/Superintendent. Not following this call-in policy will be considered a no-call / no-show event and will result in corrective or disciplinary action.You are to stay with your assigned work crew until you are reassigned by your Foreman/Superintendent.You should return all tools, carts, extension cords, ladders, etc. to your crew’s gang box or to a designated secure area at the conclusion of each work shift.  You are responsible for the tools you own.  If you leave your tools unattended on site, you take the risk for the damage or theft of your tools. Personal cell phones should not distract Employee-Owners from business tasks. They should not be used for surfing the internet or gaming during work hours. Cell phones should never be used while driving, operating equipment, or in any situation where they can cause safety hazards. Any personnel cell phone calls should be placed or returned during your lunch break or after the work shift is complete.One earbud may be allowed on GSL’s job sites, as long as it does not violate any applicable safety rules and the ambient noise level does not exceed 85db. Earbuds are not to be considered hearing protection.  Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is mandatory, and violations will not be tolerated.GSL Field Employee-Owners must follow GSL’s dress code and grooming standards as defined in GSL’s Policy Manual.GSL Field Employee-Owners are not to wear T-shirts, hard hats, etc., with logos of other electrical contractors.  You must have your first and last name printed on a label and the label should be placed and visible on the front of your hard hat.There is to be no smoking or vaping except in designated areas.Employee-Owner parking at the job sites is only allowed in designated areas.Field Employee-Owners are required to protect all finished areas.  If you see damage in your work area, report the damage, and document it before work begins in that area.  If you or other GSL Employee-Owners damage any work, equipment, or facilities you must report the damage to your direct supervisor immediately.Newly hired Field Employee-Owners are to review and sign off on the Management Directives for Field Employee-Owners during their new hire orientation.  Other Field Employee-Owners already working in the field shall also sign off on these directives.  GSL’s General Superintendents are responsible for reviewing the Management Directives with all field Employee-Owners, collecting their signed acknowledgement forms, and ensuring that the forms are placed in the Employee-Owner files.  I hereby acknowledge the following:I have been issued a copy of Great Salt Lake (GSL) Electric’s Management Directives for Field Employee-Owners.I have received a basic orientation in GSL Electric’s General Site Work Requirements. Further sitework requirements will be covered by an approved Safety Coordinator or Forman on the job site.I understand my responsibility and obligation to comply with all work requirement practices outlined in GSL’s 9.2 Management Directives for Field Employee-Owners.______________________________________________________________________________Printed Name			Signature (Employee-Owner)			Date______________________________________________________________________________GSL Electric General Superintendent						Date

Title: 9.3 Management Directives for Field Leadership
Directive: 9.3MANAGEMENT DIRECTIVES for FIELD LEADERSHIPObjectives – Field Leadership is defined as Project Foremen and Project Superintendents when applicable.  The objective of Field Leadership is to deliver their projects on-time and within budget while achieving the contractual requirements for quality and the regulatory requirements for safety.  Attitude and Self-Discipline – In addition to all of the great knowledge, experience, skills, work ethic, leadership abilities, etc., that GSL’s Field Leadership team has developed, one key requirement of GSL’s Field Leadership team is that we demonstrate a positive attitude about our company, our projects, our clients, our people, and the work we perform.  In spite of all the challenges we face, Field Leadership must have the self-discipline to refrain from engaging in negative behaviors that impact morale on our projects.  Everything GSL’s upper-management tries to do for the benefit and welfare of our employees can be undone very quickly when Field Leadership is negative and undisciplined in their behavior.  A poor attitude and undisciplined behavior by GSL’s Field Leadership will not be tolerated.  GSL’s Field Leadership must be ambassadors of good will for GSL.  We know that there are always concerns, however, the proper way to deal with these concerns is by taking these concerns to your Project Superintendent or Project Manager - not by ranting and complaining to employees or others on your projects.       Pre-planning- All projects must be pre-planned with the Project Manager. Time allowed for pre-planning will depend on time constraints, project complexity, project size, and project duration.  Projects should be planned start to finish. Once a plan has been determined, then work can proceed. Changes to the plan can be handled more efficiently than if the plan is made entirely on the fly.Execution of the Plan – Foremen and Lead Journeymen shall layout daily work activities for their crews, monitor progress during the work shift, and report quantities for their crews at the end of the shift. If the daily objectives were not met, the issues that prevented them from being completed must be reviewed and then corrective action needs to be taken.  Field Leadership is responsible to have the labor, materials, tools, and equipment, etc., available to achieve established GSL labor rate installations.  The quantities installed shall be reported and entered in the Job Plan from the Foremen or Lead Men timecards.   Project Superintendents shall monitor the performance of their Foremen.  Foremen shall monitor the performance of their Lead Men.Productivity- Foremen and Lead Men shall be accountable for the productivity of their crews.  GSL Field Foremen shall direct all GSL Electricians to operate in the most efficient manner possible and to wear their tool belts and bags for the work anticipated during the work shift.  Proper staging of materials is critical.  When possible, expediters shall distribute materials to the work areas as needed, fill up materials on field carts, etc.  Any significant labor, material, or equipment overage anticipated or discovered on a project should be reported to the Project Manager immediately. Field Leadership must focus on quality control and minimize mistakes and rework.  If you are not sure of the best means and methods to perform the work, you must check with your General Foreman or Project Manager for direction.Foreman and Lead Men are responsible report to their Project Manager and their General Superintendent on the low performing and the high performing employees working on their projects. Reporting Time - Employee timecards must be completed daily.   Time worked is to be recorded to the appropriate work codes.  Reporting Quantities - Foreman and Lead Men timecards must be completed daily with the Foremen and Lead Men hours and their crew’s installed quantities recorded accurately by cost code.  Accuracy in reporting time and quantity is paramount to effectively monitoring and controlling the project.  Job Cost versus Estimates Reports – Field leadership is to review their project’s Job Cost versus Estimates Reports at least monthly with their Project Manager.  Field Leadership must be aware of and accountable for all direct job costs. Changed Work or Changed Conditions – GSL’s Field Leadership is never to perform any changed work of significance or accept changed conditions without full consultation with and authorization from GSL’s Project Manager.  GSL’s Field Leadership shall report any concerns to their Project Manager related to any delays in the issuance of change orders for which GSL has performed or is performing the change order work.    GSL’s Field Leadership is never to assume that changes they receive in the field are just clarifications of scope already covered in the base bid.  GSL’s Project Management and GSL’s Estimating personnel will make that determination.  GSL’s Field Leadership may only proceed with changed work or perform work under changed conditions when authorized by GSL’s Project Manager.  Any project documentation received in the field must be reviewed and issued through the Project Manager.  Schedule Delays or Impacts – GSL’s Field Leadership must document in their daily reports any scheduling delays or schedule impacts that are adversely affecting GSL’ ability to effectively plan and perform their work in an efficient manner, including any quantification of lost work hours if possible.  Major changes to GSL’s planned work must be authorized by GSL’s Project Manager.  GSL’s Field Leadership does not take direction from an Owner’s Representative, from a General Contractor’s Project Manager, General Superintendent, or Sub-Contractor without GSL’s Project Management’s knowledge and approval.  Any significant changes in the project’s planned schedule must be reported to GSL’s Project Management as soon possible.Daily Reports and Project Administration Support – Through the submittal of Daily Reports, Field Leadership is responsible to provide information as soon as it is discovered regarding schedule slippage, schedule acceleration, schedule impacts, productivity impacts, work being asked to be performed outside of the contract scope, etc.  This information flows through to the Project Manager who prepares the Weekly Project Status Reports and these reports shall be submitted to the Branch Manager.  This information is time sensitive and critical in the process of getting information to the Contract Manager when needed to ensure notice and compliance provisions of the contract will be met.The financial impact to the company for failing to provide timely notice on problems in the field can be severe and ultimately may impact GSL’s performance, bonding capacity, banking relationships, and opportunities for future work.

Title: 9.4 Management Directives for General Superintendents
Directive: 9.4MANAGEMENT DIRECTIVESfor GENERAL SUPERINTENDENTSDeveloping GSL’s Work Force The Branch General Superintendent’s highest priority is to procure and help develop the best work force available for GSL’s Branch Operations through effective hiring, counseling, and training of GSL’s field personnel.  The ultimate goal is to be able to adequately staff GSL’s projects and assist Branch Management, Project Management, and GSL’s Field Leadership in achieving timely, safe, and profitable completion of their projects.  Corporate and Branch leadership shall help determine specific goals and objectives for each Branch regarding the number and quality of field leadership, the number and quality of foremen and lead men, and the number and quality of apprentices and laborers in each branch operation. To develop GSL’s work force, General Superintendents must demonstrate strong leadership, organizational and time management skills, effective communication skills, a solid understanding of GSL’s Policies and Procedures, and of local, state, and federal employment laws.   Specific work force development focus requires the following:  Coordinate with Project Management and Field Leadership to assign the desired field leadership and employees to each project when needed. Be an advocate for both GSL and for GSL’s employees in working through manpower placement, counseling, and development of individual employees. Coordinate daily with the Project Managers and Foreman on manpower needs.Attend GSL’s weekly Project Manager’s meeting to learn the latest manpower issues.Update Manpower Projections each week through Workforce Planning software. Oversee the Branch Apprenticeship Program to achieve the targeted goals for the number and quality of each apprentice level. Conduct the annual apprentice reviews and ensure that Foremen are conducting 6 month apprentice reviews. Meet the required journeyman to apprentice ratios. Track both state or county electrical licenses and continuing education requirements.Track electrical licenses in states the Branch is licensed to perform work.Coordinate with Branch Management and GSL’s Chief Operations Officer to offer training for Field Leadership and Field Employees. Administering GSL’s Work ForceTo effectively develop GSL’s work force, General Superintendents also have extensive administrative responsibilities to perform, as follows: Effective enforcement of GSL’s General Policies and Procedures.Effective enforcement of GSL’s Safety Policies and Procedures.Support Project Management and Foremen in the enforcement of Site Specific Policies and Procedures.Participate in project site visits and talks with employees and leadership as needed.Oversee GSL’s drug testing program.Review and submit timecards each week that are submitted to payroll to pay the correct number of hours at the correct rate along with any applicable subsistence or travel allowances to Branch employees.Account for every field employee’s time and notify payroll of missing employee’s hours or timesheets.Account for every field employee’s time and notify human resources payroll of missing employee’s hours or time sheets that affect benefits.Review and approve field employees Cash Expense reports and Visa reports.Review and approve employee’s vehicle reimbursements.Oversee the management of GSL’s vehicle fleet i.e.; repairs, purchase of vehicles,and annual registration of vehicles.

Title: 9.5 Management Directives for Project Management
Directive: 9.5GSL MANAGEMENT DIRECTIVESfor PROJECT MANAGEMENTContract ReviewScope -  In each contract signed by GSL Electric, the Scope of Work shall include the work set forth in GSL’s bid, proposal, or description of work.  GSL’s proposal or a suitable description of the scope of work, including all bid clarifications, inclusions, and exclusions, must be expressly incorporated and made a part of the Contract Documents between the Contractor and GSL Electric.  GSL’s scope of work must also be consistent with the Prime Agreement between the General Contractor and the Owner.Clarifications and Exclusions -  When GSL Electric is the successful bidder on a project, Branch Management and Project Management shall review with Estimating to ensure that all clarifications and exclusions in GSL’s Bid Proposal are specifically identified in the contract to be signed by GSL – unless the clarifications and exclusions have been addressed prior to execution of the contract with an appropriate adjustment to the contract price or the scope of the contract is otherwise reconciled to the bid proposal.  Schedule Analysis -  It is imperative that in addition to the scope review issues listed above, a schedule analysis be performed prior to establishing the bid price and submitting the bid proposal.  If a schedule is not included in the bid documents, estimators shall immediately request a copy of the schedule showing as much detail as possible.  An electronic schedule that shows the work activity relationships is preferred to a PDF schedule.  The Operations Team must have the opportunity to review the schedule and determine whether to pursue the project.  When a bid is to be submitted, determine what cost impacts need to be addressed with an aggressive project schedule or an elongated project schedule.Addendums to Contracts -  GSL’s Business Managers must review the General Conditions and Special Conditions of every contract or purchase order for construction services for work to be provided by GSL and strive to implement all GSL’s Contract Addendum provisions.  When this is not possible, the following Contract Addendum provisions are critical and must be included in any contract or purchase order that GSL executes. Lien / Bond Rights -  Notwithstanding any provision to the contrary, Subcontractor may take all steps necessary to preserve and enforce its lien and bond rights and nothing contained herein shall constitute a waiver of Subcontractor’s right to file a mechanic’s lien or bond claim.Payment and Performance Bonds -  General Contractor shall only be permitted to request Payment and Performance Bonds from Subcontractor at the time of contract award to Subcontractor and if Subcontractor received proper notice in the bid documents that Payment and Performance Bonds were required as a condition precedent to an award of the Subcontract. Releases -  Any form or contract language wherein the Subcontractor purports to release the Contractor, Owner or Design Professional is hereby qualified by the following language whether or not the Subcontractor specifically adds the language: “This release shall apply only to work for which payment has been received in full by Subcontractor; shall not apply to retention; shall not apply to unbilled changes; shall not apply to claims which have been asserted in writing or which have not yet become known to Subcontractor; and, shall be conditional upon receipt of funds to Subcontractor’s account.” Contract Summary -  GSL’s Project Manager’s shall refer to and follow the contract provisions for the General Terms and Conditions and any Special Terms and Conditions as identified in the Contract Summary for both GSL’s contract with the General Contractor and the Prime Agreement between the General Contractor and the Owner (see Job Monitoring). Subcontracts -  GSL’s Project Managers shall ensure that every subcontract or purchase order for construction services issued by GSL shall bind GSL’s subcontractors to all contract documents and provisions required of GSL Electric.  Formal subcontracts shall be issued for amounts over $50,000.00.  Project Managers are to use either the GSL Standard Subcontract or the GSL Preferred Subcontract. These subcontracts are in the Projects Folder under Templates/ Standard Subcontract or Preferred Subcontract.    Project Pre-Planning and Developing the Construction PlanProject Turnover Meetings -  GSL’s Contract Manager, Branch Manager, Project Manager and Project Field Leadership shall meet with GSL’s estimators to review the bid documents and contract documents and review a pre-construction checklist that identifies all contractual requirements with associated notice requirements or completion dates of the contract.  Manpower and Field Leadership Plan - A project organization chart shall be prepared, and delegation level review shall be conducted for all field leadership and key individuals assigned to the project.  The project organization chart shall be updated during the various phases of the project and the current organization chart shall be posted in the job trailer.  The schedule’s milestones and completion dates shall be reviewed in detail.  A man-loaded schedule shall be prepared and a schedule of values with appropriate cost allocations and completion times shall be established.   Prefabrication - Project Management shall review each of their projects and proactively determine the scope of work that can effectively be prefabricated to save labor, improve efficiency/productivity and installation time on their projects.  Project Managers shall direct and coordinate with GSL’s pre-fabrication team as needed to produce the materials and assemblies on their projects.  BIM Modeling shall be utilized as much as possible to pre-plan the layout of the raceway systems.     Submittals and Purchasing -  Project Management shall prepare the project’s required submittals in a time consistent with the project scheduling requirements.  Project Management shall prepare and issue the purchase orders and subcontracts on their projects with the goal of meeting or saving on the project’s budgeted costs for materials, subcontract work, equipment rentals, or other miscellaneous project costs.  The goal is for Project Management to buy out 80 to 90 percent of the project.  Project Management shall schedule the release of their materials as needed to meet the requirements of the project schedule, Project Management will coordinate with GSL’s Purchasing Department and GSL’s Field Leadership to purchase basic commodity items needed on their projects.    Executing the Construction PlanField Leadership and Manpower Requirements – GSL’s Project Managers shall coordinate with their Branch Manager, their Branch General Superintendent, and their Branch Safety Superintendent to ensure that the best available field leadership, labor, and safety coordinators are assigned to their projects. Scheduling - Due to labor shortages, the ever-increasing pace of construction, delays with predecessor performance, and material delivery lead times, scheduling is the number one problem in our industry.  Project Managers must take the initiative on project scheduling – request a sit down with the GC and talk.  Once we are under contract, we need to analyze the schedule, looking at lead times, and understanding the value of a day lost on the schedule (per man per day).  Have this number ready to present to the GC in the event of a delay.Work with your GF or Foremen to proactively use look ahead schedules and utilize them in the project coordination meetings.  Be prepared for those meetings to make your case on when predecessor work needs to be completed so that we can do our work in an efficient manner.  Get commitments on work to be completed, get specific.   Break look ahead schedules down by activity and man load the activities.  Identify beginning dates for the activity and the normal duration required to complete the activity.  Participate early on, communicate regularly and often, be very incremental.  Always begin with the end in mind.  Utilize Pull Planning by milestone during the project.Job Monitoring - GSL’s Project Managers shall focus on executing the plan and allow for sufficient job site time to monitor the proper performance of the planned work.  The Project Manager is responsible for the job’s performance.  GSL’s Project Management shall be aware of all aspects of the Contract Summary including the notice provisions and the required scope of work.  The Project Managers shall review the daily reports, prepare the Weekly Project Status Reports, and communicate with GSL’s Contract Managers on any delays, disruptions, significant scope changes, lack of timely change order approvals, etc., that are experienced on their projects.      Job Plans – It is critically important that project Job Plans are utilized to track labor hour trends and analyze on-going project productivity. Tracking labor productivity by comparing budgeted labor hours by work code to actual hours by work code allows the Project Manager to determine positive or negative labor hour variances.  Determining labor hour variances allows for this information to be used to estimate labor hour projections to complete by work code and cumulatively to project labor hours to complete the project.  Job plans must be updated at least monthly to account for change orders and other budget adjustments or the Job Plan will be ineffective as a tool to address labor performance and project labor hours and costs.  It is essential that Project Managers make adjustments as necessary with project manpower, work crews, project leadership, materials, tools, equipment, training, subcontractor performance, safety, etc., to keep the project within budget.  Job Costs / Estimates Report -  GSL’s Project Management shall share the GSL’s Job Costs / Estimates Report with their Field Leadership weekly to help ensure that Field Leadership is fully aware of their project’s budgeted direct job costs versus their project’s actual direct job costs to date. Job Site Visits -  Minimum twice per month every week if possible.  Out-of-town projects minimum once a month, twice a month if possible.   During a job site visit, check in with the General Contractor or Owner, express appreciation and encourage our Employee-Owners, help build moral on the job site, check on the performance of the job, help solve problems and support your field leadership.  Visit the job site with a purpose …Interfacing with the General Contractor or Owner’s Representative -  Project Managers are to meet regularly with the General Contractor’s Project Manager or the Owner’s representative to obtain feedback on GSL’s performance, request information or coordinate assistance, response on RFI’s, submittals, change order approvals, etc.  Contract Changes -  GSL’s Project Management can only accept scope changes from the party we are directly contracted with.  In most cases this will be the Owner or General Contractor (but not on the same job).  This means we do not take direction either verbally or by receiving updated drawings or other documents from an Owner’s or General Contractor’s representative, their design team or their other subcontractors on the project.  Any directions received from any party besides the party GSL is contracted to shall not be acted upon without written authorization from the contracting party.Document Control -  All bid documents must be identified, numbered, and recorded in GSL’s Project Document Control Log.  After award of a new project, all updated drawings, submittals, etc., Project Management must log in the updated documents and compare them to the previous information provided to determine the scope and pricing changes associated with the updated release of new documents.  Caution must be taken to review all documents submitted electronically or placed in a drop box.  Project Management shall control updated documents and place documents into Plan Grid for use in the field.  Major releases shall be reviewed by GSL’s Project Management, with support from GSL’s Estimating Department as needed, to determine the scope and impact of any changes.  When new documents are issued that means something has changed and it is imperative that Project Management determines what those changes are and what cost or scheduling impacts, they will have on GSL.  GSL’s Project Management must notify the General Contractor or the Owner of the associated impacts of the change within the time periods allowed in the contract documents. Upon the receipt of any new documents, a notice must be issued to the Owner or General Contractor stating that there may be cost impacts to GSL and that the updated information will be reviewed, and any cost impacts will be identified and disclosed as required by the contract documents. If extensions of time are required to review the changes in updated documents, notices shall be issued to the Owner of General Contractor informing them of the estimated date on which the review can be completed.Change Order Requests and Change Order Management -  Project Management is to submit timely, accurate, and detailed change order requests as needed and within the time requirements as outlined in the contract documents.  Project Management is to follow-up on pending change orders and ensure the timely approval of the COR’s submitted on a project.  Time Extensions - Regardless of whether the contract documents prohibit time extensions for additional or changed work, GSL should always request time extensions when necessary but especially when the project has a liquidated damages provision that can be assessed for delays.Weekly Project Status Reports -  GSL’s Project Management is required to submit a Weekly Project Status Report to the party we are contracted to.  GSL believes that this is a value-added service that assists the Owner or General Contractor as well as GSL Electric in facilitating communication and follow-through on outstanding issues or current issues that need to be addressed.  Progress Billings, Job Plan Updates, and Job Cost Projections -  Project Management should regularly review and follow GSL’s Standard Operating Procedures.  Project Managers shall complete and submit their progress billings, job plan updates, change order cost breakdowns, budget adjustments, and job cost projections monthly by the required contract dates.  GSL’s Project Management shall strive to submit progress billings sufficient to keep their projects in a positive cash flow position by avoiding under billings (when actual job costs plus earned to date overhead and profit are less than progress billings submitted to date). Project Managers shall stive to accurately project job costs at completion to stay focused on the jobs actual costs compared to the budget to achieve the targeted gross profit margins on each project.    Project Managers shall reinforce the procedure that Field Leadership is responsible for laying out their crew daily, defining what work is expected to be accomplished that day, facilitate the work to be completed by securing the necessary labor, leadership, materials, and equipment.  At the end of the shift, and then checking back to determine what was accomplished during the day and record the progress made on the Foreman’s timecard.  Based on the results achieved, make any adjustments necessary when planning the next day’s work. Project Closeout GSL shall submit the following documents upon completion of their projects: Field Leadership InterviewsOperations and Maintenance ManualsLetter of Warranty Final Progress and Retention BillingEmployee EvaluationsGeneral Contractor or Owner Survey

Title: 9.7 Management Directives for Estimating
Directive: 9.7MANAGEMENT DIRECTIVESfor ESTIMATINGThe primary objective for the estimating department is to produce accurate and timely estimates as directed by Branch Management.  GSL’s estimates should reflect the lowest cost means and methods to perform the work that satisfies the requirements of the bid documents. Pre-Bid DirectivesGreat contractors systematically and strategically approach each bid.  A great piece of contractor advice is: “If you are going to bid a job, always find at least three unique advantages.”  You have to work the bid and not just go through the motions of tabulating the numbers. When developing an estimate, consider the following:Bid Projects from an entrepreneurial perspective.  Be sure GSL’s costs are covered but always search for lowest cost means and methods that will meet the specifications of the bid.  Search diligently and find the GSL advantages.  Be cautious when using job plan data to determine install rates.  We have to use competitive labor units.  Know who the competition is and try to determine how they may be looking at the project.Be aware of what our competitor’ advantages may be, such as electricals who do their own excavating, or contractors who are bidding both mechanical and electrical.Make recommendations to Branch Management when it is apparent that GSL may need to alter its normal cost structure in order to be competitive on a project, ie., costing out company owned equipment.Check with architects, suppliers, and subcontractors to be sure we aware of all GC’s who are bidding the project.  Bid to all GC’s unless we have an exclusive teaming arrangement with a particular GC.Partner when possible with General Contractors, Suppliers and Subcontractors to help identify advantages for GSL.Know which projects are being targeted by GSL.  Work with Branch Management to determine how we obtain best pricing from suppliers and subcontractors.  Be sure we are getting competitive quotes.  Determine who will take the lead in negotiating pricing with suppliers and subcontractors.Provide deductive alternatives whenever possible, even when not allowed by specification.  Don’t give too much information on deductive alternatives prior to contract award (keep this information within GSL until project award).When using 50 or 60 hour workweeks in the base bid, do not disclose this information or GSL will have a more difficult negotiating for overtime when we are being impacted by change orders or by scheduling issues.Be mindful of how we fill out bid forms as it relates to the schedule of values and think about how the schedule of values may impact billings and cash flow on the project.Find opportunities in the drawings to build the project more efficiently.Work with pre-construction services to find pre-fabrication opportunities in order to lower bid costs and to maximize available manpower. Work with experienced Project Superintendents and Foremen to find value engineering opportunities. Determine unique ways to save general conditions versus how others might approach the work. Lead Estimators shall coordinate the estimating activities for the electrical take-off. All bids over $2.0 million must have a pre-bid evaluation form completed with as much information as possible and then reviewed with Branch Management and emailed to the Executive Committee, with a comment deadline, before beginning the take-off and preparing the bid proposal.Early in the take-off process, estimators shall submit timely RFI’s in order to sufficiently clarify the scope of work to be included in the estimate.  Any RFI’s that are not responded to shall be listed in the bid proposal and GSL shall identify what actions GSL has taken regarding the RFI’s that were not responded to (scope items included, excluded, allowances given, etc.).  All estimates must clearly state its exclusions or clarifications in the bid proposal.  If a bid does not cover 100% of the electrical work anticipated for a full and complete operating system, GSL’s proposal must clearly state what has been excluded from our estimate.  Estimators shall not include exclusions or clarifications that do not apply to a specific project.  Estimators must complete the Estimating Checklist prior to the bid review.It is not sufficient to state that our price is based solely on information contained in the “E” Drawings. All cost impacts documented in the specifications must be accounted for including general conditions, special conditions, etc.  GSL will be bound to all documents, all drawings (including mechanical and architectural drawings), and all specifications, regardless of the discipline or specification section.As needed, other discipline’s documents must be thoroughly reviewed for electrical scope.  For instance, mechanical and plumbing drawings should always be checked for duct detectors, heat trace, and other items that could have a cost impact to GSL but are not shown in the electrical drawings. Architectural drawings should be reviewed and referred to for building height, specific dimensions, reflected ceiling plans etc.  For industrial projects, all P&ID’s must be thoroughly reviewed and all take-off accounted for.  The contract will tie us to all drawings included in the RFP.  If estimators have questions, do not understand a specific system, or in general are not comfortable bidding a certain project or portion of a project, they must ask for assistance.  They will receive guidance on how to complete the take-off or another estimator may be assigned to help out with the estimate.  It is never permissible to guess if we are bidding something correctly.  If there is a question, or even a doubt, use all available resources in order to get the answers needed before proceeding with the bid.Value engineering alternates should be developed and included in the estimate as needed or allowed to ensure that the lowest cost scope, means, and methods are considered and offered to the client.  Value engineering examples would be proposing alternates for aluminum feeders, alternate lighting packages, alternates for MC Cable, etc.  It is imperative that in addition to the scope review issues listed above, that a schedule analysis be performed prior to establishing the bid price and submitting the bid proposal.  If a schedule is not included in the bid documents, estimators shall immediately request a copy of the schedule showing as much detail as possible.    The Branch Manager must have the opportunity to review the schedule and determine whether to pursue the project.  If a bid is to be submitted on a project with an aggressive schedule, cost impacts and labor requirements will need to be assessed. Branch Management’s Bid Review ConsiderationsAfter reviewing the out of the box Overhead and Profit and the Labor Risk Ratio, find the appropriate mix of these variables to submit bids that are priced competitively with acceptable levels of risk.Consider leadership and manpower constraints.  Consider impacts to productivity and costs associated with the use of temporary labor companies.Until special assembly pricing can be used to price pre-fab work, utilize an estimate of the percentage of man hours utilizing pre-fab & apply an estimate of lower wage rates for the pre-fab work to these man hours in order to lower GSL’s labor costs. Consider modifying company owned equipment costs when necessary.    Consider using tax savings as necessary to be competitive.Be mindful of project duration and complexity.Look carefully at potential labor, material, and subcontractor cost escalations during the project duration.Be mindful of covering overheads through the procurement of sufficient and steady backlog. Be mindful of keeping our work force engaged in times of severe labor shortages.Post Award DirectivesWhen a project has been awarded, if GSL was not successful, get as much information as possible on what the successful bidder did to capture the project.  This information can be very valuable to GSL in bidding future projects. When GSL Electric is the successful bidder on a project, the estimating department shall review with Branch Management & Project Management to ensure that all clarifications & exclusions in GSL’s bid proposal are specifically identified in the contract to be signed by GSL - unless the clarifications and exclusions have been addressed prior to execution of the contract with an appropriate adjustment to the contract price or the scope of the contract is otherwise reconciled to the bid proposal.The estimating department shall participate in the Project Turn-Over Meeting with the Operations Project Management team following the Turn-Over Meeting Agenda and reviewing the items identified in the Project Turn-Over Checklist.  The means and methods utilized in the take-off of the project shall be thoroughly reviewed with the project management team.  Every exclusion or clarification in the bid shall be reviewed.  All pre-fabrication incorporated in the project shall be reviewed.In the Project Turn-Over Meeting, all value engineering options shall be reviewed. All major vendors and subcontractors shall be discussed.  The construction schedule and interim milestones shall be reviewed.  GSL’s field leadership and manpower requirements shall be reviewed.  GSL’s Contract Summary is also to be reviewed in the turn-over meeting.The Estimating Department shall ensure that all bid documents are identified, numbered and available in the estimating folder.   Upon award of a project, the bid documents can then be moved to the job folder and to Plan Grid in order to clearly identify the scope of the project and to provide information to effectively manage the change order process. Design Assist estimates coming from the Estimating Department must involve review by the Engineering and Design Build Department in formulating a bid price.  If the project is awarded, the Design Build Department should be involved in reviewing change orders, ASI’s, etc., as the project develops.After contract award, if new documents are issued, that means something has changed and it is imperative that GSL determines what those changes are and what cost or scheduling impacts they will have on GSL.  As directed by the Branch Manager, major releases of new information may need to be reviewed by GSL’s Estimating Department and Project Management in order to determine the scope and impact of any changes.  This may include participating in the pricing of major change orders to the conformed set of drawings (or Issued for Construction (IFC) drawings).  All updated drawings or other information must be reviewed against the previous set of drawings and information to determine scope and pricing changes. Once changes have been identified and quantified, GSL’s Project Management is able to notify the General Contractor or the Owner of the associated impacts of the change.

Directive: 9.14MANAGEMENT DIRECTIVES for CONTRACT MANAGERSObjectives of Contract Management – Contract Managers are to oversee contract compliance at the branch level, report to GSL’s Executive Committee any operational concerns on projects, and ensure that GSL leadership is aware of and strictly following the notice and compliance provisions of the contracts. Contract Manager’s Role – Contract Managers are to provide checks and balances to our operations team. The goal of the Contract Manager is to timely identify project problems, provide timely notice and cost impacts, and try to resolve the problems expeditiously without having to resort to the filing of a formal claim. Tasks to be Performed by Contract Managers – Ensure that both the Prime Agreement and GSL’s contract are reviewed simultaneously during contract review and prior to execution of GSL’s contract.After negotiations, and following the execution of the contract, ensure that a complete Contract Summary has been prepared for both agreements.Ensure that Subcontracts and Purchase Orders issued by GSL on each project include the Prime Agreement and GSL’s Contract as part of the Subcontract or Purchase Order Agreements.   Ensure that the Contract Summary is distributed to the Title: 9.16 Management Directives for Purchasing
Directive:
9.16
MANAGEMENT DIRECTIVES FOR PURCHASING


Procurement is one of the most important activities in project management is to properly purchase the materials and to align the subcontractors on the project. Our ultimate goal is to procure the materials at the same value or less than what we had at bid day. By buying the project out 100% reduces the potential risk of material escalation. The following is a procedure that will help you understand what is expected of the PM and others that support the project management process.
• The Purchasing Vision o Pre-planning Process
 PM is to work with the Foreman that is assigned to the project and develop a take off reflecting the way they are going to stage and  build the job incorporating all of the Value Engineering, Pre-Fab, manufacturing ideas, and the re-routing of duct banks and conduit racks etc. After the take off is complete a bill of materials for commodities such as fittings, supports nuts bolts should be developed.
o Master Purchase Orders
 Quoted materials should be in•unediately re-quantified and verified and P.O.'s should be developed with the following information. (All of the points listed below need to be line items on the Purchase Order)
Accurate quantities of materials
Required Delivery information o Date Required on the site o Proper Address o Submittals that are required as well as a copy of the specifications that are needed to supply the right information on the submittal. Plus the date that the submittal is required along with the required number of copies
 Include in the PO a list of all of the required spare parts and the O&M manuals if required.
 All required start-up support that is required needs to be clearly stated in the Purchase order.
The total cost of the purchase order needs to be verified as well as the cost of materials in the case additional material is required.
Make sure that Sales Tax at the appropriate rate is included. If the job is tax-exempt the required tax-exempt number needs to be filed in the office.
Make sure that the ancillary parts are included on the PO such as lamps, batteries, spare parts if applicable etc.
 Subcontracts
If the contract is $10,000.00 or more a Subcontract needs to be prepared and executed.
All sales tax or fees need to be included in their total contract amount or negotiated prior to contract execution.  The scope of work needs to be included in detail and assure that it is the same as or exceeds the expectation of the drawings and specification.
A subcontractor is anyone performing work in behalf of GSL Electric on a project. i.e. Low voltage contractors, instrumentation, engineering and design, lightning protection. Etc.
 Commodities
Conduit/ wire/ fittings/ support materials/ etc.
All commodities need to be identified after the PM and foreman take-off is complete. A bill of materials needs to be established. At which time contact the vendor of choice to support an inventory control system in a conex to assure that we only buy what we need and return in good order what was overstocked.
All quantities and unit prices as well as how long these prices are good for (possibly the duration of the project) needs to be stated in the purchase order.
 General Expenses and rental equipment
Determine what equipment and tools that will be required for the project and the timing of when the tools and equipment will be needed based upon a working schedule. Issue a PO based on the needs stated above.
 The submittal process o Scour through the specification and determine all of the items in each specifications section that need to be submitted on prior to finalizing the PO copy that portion of the specification entitled submittal in each section and submit this information with our purchase order to the vendor or the Subconfractor to assure a smooth tansition will occur during the submittal process. It is the PM's responsibility to assure and check each submittal prior to transmitting them to the General Confractor or the owner. With highly sophisticated engineers and owners it may be prudent to have a presubmittal review to create an atmosphere of cooperation and completeness.
All submittals are to be logged in and tacked through the Viewpoint Software.
 Every time a submittal is given to the GC or the owner a letter of transmittal is required to be attached with a signed copy returned to the project file.
Always retain one copy for our records that reflect the approved submittal. o No item being submitted on is to be released for shipment or manufacturing until such time that the submittal is approved with no notations, if there are notations but approved all notations are to be tansmitted to the vendor to make such modifications prior to manufacturing or shipping.
Issuing purchase orders o Attached are the procedures for dealing with purchase orders and entering them in to Viewpoint software.
o Philosophy of purchasing equipment.
 Choose the most cost effective vendor.
 Low price isn't always the cheapest or the most cost effective.  Verify that the bills of materials all as equal and meet the specification and the intent of the project.
Re-assure that the O&M manuals spare parts etc. are not in addition to the quote.
Prior to issuing PO's we need to make sure that we have completed the internal Value Engineering to assure that we are not purchasing parts that may be changed next week.  If at all possible we need to support the Vendors that support us on bid day. (Not at all costs but if they are close give them the benefit of the doubt) This is strictly a judgment call.
 Insure that commodities such as wire, and conduit at times, that the terms and conditions and freight are allowed if at all possible. Obviously if it is a small job it will be local shipments.

PROBLEMS NEED TO BE IMMEDIATELY DEALT WITH
AFTER AWARD OR A FIRM LETTER OF INTENT. THESE DECISIONS WILL NEED BRANCH MANAGEMENT APPROVAL AND m CASES CORPORATE APPROVAL.
 Advantages of Pre-Buyout
 PW Foreman can verify the cost of the materials vs. the estimate o The foreman can spend his or her time running the job rather than running for parts.
PM can control the risk of escalation.
Productivity of crew 	increase due to the availability of material.

Title: Management Directives for Leadman Levels 1-3
Directive:
MANAGEMENT DIRECTIVES for LEADMAN LEVELS 1 THROUGH 3
Objectives:
The objective of Leadmen at GSL Electric is to assist Foremen and Field Leadership in delivering projects on-time, within budget, while maintaining high standards for safety and quality. Leadmen are responsible for overseeing specific tasks and crew activities on job sites, ensuring efficiency, safety, and adherence to project specifications.
Attitude and Self-Discipline:
Leadmen, like all GSL Field Leadership, must exhibit a positive attitude toward GSL, its projects, employees, and clients. Negativity and lack of discipline can quickly undermine morale and project efficiency. Leadmen are expected to handle concerns by communicating directly with their Foreman or Project Manager, not by airing grievances on the job site.
A poor attitude or undisciplined behavior will not be tolerated. Leadmen must act as ambassadors of goodwill and exhibit professionalism and self-discipline at all times.
Pre-Planning:
Leadmen are involved in the pre-planning phase of each project in collaboration with the Foreman or Project Manager. This includes planning daily and weekly tasks, identifying necessary materials and resources, and preparing for the efficient execution of work. Pre-planning minimizes delays and allows for flexibility when changes occur.
Execution of the Plan:
Leadmen shall assist in laying out daily work activities for their crews, monitoring progress, and reporting completed tasks to the Foreman at the end of each shift. If tasks are not completed as planned, the Leadman must review the issues, take corrective action, and report these actions to the Foreman.
Leadmen are also responsible for ensuring that labor, materials, tools, and equipment are available for each task. The quantities installed shall be recorded accurately and reported at the end of each shift.
Productivity:
Leadmen must ensure their crew operates as efficiently as possible. This includes proper task assignment, material staging, and tool preparation. Leadmen are expected to manage crew productivity by ensuring that electricians wear the necessary tools for their tasks and that materials are readily available.
If any significant overage in labor, material, or equipment is anticipated, the Leadman must report this to the Foreman or Project Manager immediately. Leadmen are responsible for minimizing rework and ensuring that work is performed correctly the first time.
Reporting Time and Quantities:
Leadmen must complete their timecards daily, recording both their own and their crew’s hours and installed quantities by cost code. Accuracy in reporting is essential for project monitoring and controlling.
Job Cost versus Estimates Reports:
Leadmen must collaborate with the Foreman to review the project’s Job Cost versus Estimates Reports, at least monthly. Leadmen must understand how their tasks impact project costs and work to maintain alignment with the budget.
Changed Work or Changed Conditions:
Leadmen are not authorized to make decisions regarding significant changes in scope or project conditions. All changes must be reviewed and approved by the Foreman or Project Manager before work proceeds. Leadmen are responsible for reporting any concerns related to delays or changes in work scope to the Foreman.
Schedule Delays or Impacts:
Leadmen must report any scheduling delays, impacts, or inefficiencies that may affect the project timeline. These delays should be documented in daily reports and communicated to the Foreman and Project Manager. Leadmen are not to accept direction from external parties without GSL management's knowledge and approval.
Daily Reports and Project Administration Support:
Leadmen must provide timely and accurate information through Daily Reports, detailing any issues that impact schedule, productivity, or project scope. This information is critical for the Foreman and Project Manager to assess project progress and address any concerns.
Failing to provide accurate and timely information can result in significant financial and operational impacts to GSL Electric, potentially affecting future opportunities and project performance.
